newsitem.title: USA: Argentine bond's success allays supply fears.
newsitem.headline: Argentine bond's success allays supply fears.

text.p: Argentina's $2 billion global bond selling without a hitch allayed fears that an oversupply of new issues would strain the market of emerging debts, analysts and traders said.
Market participants were encouraged by the enthusiasm with which investors greeted the Argentine offer after the $1 billion 10-year global bond placed by Mexico last week.
"Some people had been worried about the timing," said Ingrid Iverson, emerging market debt strategist at UBS Securities. "But it turned out to be well oversubscribed."

Over 300 accounts participated in the global deal, with 70 percent from the U.S., 15 percent from Europe, nine percent from Asia and six percent from Latin America, said a source from co-lead manager J.P. Morgan, noting that a "significant portion" were first-time buyers.
The global bond has attracted a large pool of crossover buyers from global bond funds and high-yield bond funds, confirmed Richard Luddington, head of J.P. Morgan's Emerging Markets Syndicate desk.
The large and liquid global bonds issued from emerging markets are increasingly eclipsing the Brady bonds, which are repackaged bad loans, as the new focus of the debt market, he said.
Market sources said the dazzling 40 percent return from emerging market debt investment last year had a profound impact on enticing new investors to emerging markets.
Reflecting the hearty demand for the Argentine issue, price talk on the deal went from 500 basis points (bp) over U.S. Treasuries to 475 bp to the final 462.5 bp.
Argentina also scrapped the five-year bond offer in the original two-tranche deal to raise the entire $2 billion in the 20-year tranche, they said.
"Because of its size, we expect it to become a benchmark," Miguel Kiguel, Argentine Undersecretary of Finance, told Reuters after the pricing of the deal.

Investors' demand for longer maturity meshed well with Argentina's debt management preference, and Argentine officials are considering the issuance of 30-year dollar bonds, depending on the tradeoff between the maturity and the interest cost, he said.
Kiguel reiterated a statement from the government that the country plans to raise another $1 billion, likely denominated in German marks, in the international capital market in the first quarter.
After the new bond was freed to trade on the secondary market, it rose from par to trade as high as 102-1/4 before sliding to 101-1/4 bid in early afternoon, a trading source said.

The euphoria in the Latin debt market following the two successful megabond deals from Mexico and Argentina totalling $3 billion could evaporate quickly if the U.S. Treasury yields spiked up, warned market sources.
"Right now, investing in emerging market debt instruments represents Treasury risk not sovereign risk," said a fund manager.
"We don't see any problems from any major Latin American countries," she said. "The risk lies in the Treasuries."
